what_it_does: Neutral-atom quantum computers arrange individual atoms as qubits in distinct zones — a storage area where atoms wait, an entangling area where two-qubit operations happen, and a readout zone where results are measured. Moving atoms between zones takes time and degrades quality (fidelity), so a good compiler must plan those movements carefully. This paper introduces ZAC (Zoned Architecture Compiler), which treats 'qubit reuse' as a first-class scheduling goal: if an atom just finished an operation in the entangling zone and another operation is immediately needed, ZAC keeps it there instead of sending it back to storage and fetching it again. The compiler also introduces smart atom placement strategies that anticipate which atoms will be needed next, a new scheduling algorithm tailored to zoned machines, and a formal description language that can model many different zoned quantum hardware designs. On tested circuits, the approach reportedly achieves up to 22x better fidelity than compiling for a single undivided zone.
